issues.legal_issue: The amendment abolishing a landlord’s right to resume tenanted land and vesting tenancy land for transfer to cultivating tenants does not violate the Constitution’s basic structure.
material_facts: The amendment ended the landlord’s right to resume tenanted land, including where the landlord bona fide required it for personal cultivation and relied on its income for maintenance.
The amendment provided for tenancy land to vest in the State and for cultivating tenants to obtain occupancy rights.
The law was challenged as not being agrarian reform and as violating the Constitution’s basic structure.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was a law aimed at agrarian reform and securing the Directive Principles in Articles 39(b) and (c); it did not offend the basic structure of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Articles 31-A, 31-B and 31-C, Article 39(b) and (c), and the principles stated in Waman Rao v. Union of India and Kesavananda Bharati. It held that transferring land ownership to the tiller is a means of using a community resource for the common good and that preferring a cultivating tenant over a landlord who did not personally cultivate the land is part of agrarian reform.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law that reforms agricultural landholding or tenancy.
predicates.tenant_personally_cultivates_land: A tenant personally cultivates the land at issue.
predicates.landlord_did_not_personally_cultivate_la: The landlord did not personally cultivate the land at issue.
predicates.law_transfers_tenancy_land_for_cultivato: The law provides for tenancy land to be transferred for ownership by the person cultivating it.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns agrarian reform that transfers land from a non-cultivating landlord to its cultivating tenant, the law does not violate the basic structure.

issues.legal_issue: A lay tribunal with members whose qualifications are unspecified is not invalid merely because some disputes may be important or some tribunals have functioned poorly, where the assigned disputes do not require a trained judicial mind.
material_facts: The law created land tribunals with members nominated by the government and did not specify qualifications for those members.
The tribunals were assigned disputes concerning applications for registration as an occupant.
Some tribunals had been reported to function inefficiently or without observing proper procedures.
The court found that the disputes assigned to the tribunals did not require the application of a trained judicial mind.
issues.conclusion: The tribunal provisions were not invalidated by the absence of specified qualifications or by the malfunctioning of some tribunals.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished disputes that require a trained judicial mind from those that do not. The poor functioning of some tribunals does not by itself invalidate the statutory provisions establishing tribunals or assigning disputes to them.

predicates.challenge_to_lay_tribunal_structure: A party challenged a statutory tribunal because it was not required to consist of trained judicial personnel.
predicates.assigned_disputes_do_not_require_trained: The disputes assigned to the tribunal can be decided without applying a trained judicial mind.
predicates.tribunal_members_have_no_specified_quali: The law does not specify qualifications for some or all tribunal members.
predicates.some_tribunals_function_poorly: Some tribunals have performed their functions inefficiently or improperly.

issues.definition: A challenge to a lay tribunal does not invalidate its structure when the assigned disputes do not require a trained judicial mind, even if qualifications are unspecified and some tribunals function poorly.

issues.legal_issue: A state-law restriction cannot prevent advocates from appearing before statutory tribunals when it conflicts with parliamentary law governing the right of advocates to practise.
material_facts: The law barred legal practitioners from appearing in proceedings before the tribunals.
The restriction conflicted with parliamentary provisions concerning advocates’ rights of appearance.
The State Legislature was not competent to make a law repugnant to parliamentary law on the relevant subject.
issues.conclusion: The restriction was not to be enforced so as to prevent advocates from appearing before the tribunals.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 30 of the Advocates Act, 1961, and Section 14 of the Indian Bar Councils Act, 1926, and relied on Entries 77 and 78 of List I of the Seventh Schedule. It adopted the reasoning in Jaswant Kaur v. State of Haryana that the state-law restriction was repugnant to parliamentary law.

predicates.challenge_to_appearance_bar_before_statu: A party challenged a restriction on advocates appearing in proceedings before a statutory tribunal.
predicates.state_law_excludes_advocates: A state law bars advocates from appearing before the tribunal.
predicates.parliamentary_law_grants_advocates_appea: Parliamentary law grants advocates a right of appearance that conflicts with the state-law restriction.

issues.definition: When a state-law bar on advocates appearing before a tribunal conflicts with a parliamentary law granting that right, advocates may appear before the tribunal.

issues.legal_issue: Completed tribunal decisions need not be reopened solely because legal practitioners were prevented from appearing in the proceedings.
material_facts: Tribunals had already rendered decisions in proceedings in which legal practitioners were not allowed to appear.
The Court considered whether those decisions should be reopened on that ground.
issues.conclusion: The decisions already rendered by the tribunals did not need to be reopened solely because legal practitioners had been prevented from appearing.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that it was not necessary to reopen decisions already rendered on the ground that legal practitioners had not been allowed to appear before the tribunals.

predicates.request_to_reopen_completed_tribunal_pro: A party seeks to reopen a proceeding in which a tribunal has already rendered its decision.
predicates.advocates_were_prevented_from_appearing: Legal practitioners were not allowed to appear in the completed proceeding.

issues.definition: A completed tribunal decision is not reopened solely because legal practitioners were prevented from appearing in the proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional challenge to agrarian-reform legislation need not require reconsideration of an earlier constitutional precedent when the challenge can be resolved without revisiting it.
material_facts: A party argued that an earlier decision concerning constitutional provisions and legislation placed in the protected schedule should be reconsidered.
The Court determined that it could decide the case without reconsidering or going behind that decision.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not reconsider or go behind the earlier decision for the purposes of the case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Waman Rao v. Union of India, which addressed Articles 31-A, 31-B and 31-C and challenges to laws included in the Ninth Schedule, and noted the basic-structure principle in Kesavananda Bharati. It held that reconsideration was unnecessary to decide the case.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: A party challenges the constitutionality of a law concerning agrarian reform.
predicates.existing_precedent_addresses_the_control: An earlier decision addresses the constitutional principles relevant to the challenge.
predicates.case_can_be_decided_without_revisiting_p: The court can decide the case without reconsidering or departing from the earlier decision.

issues.definition: When an agrarian-reform constitutional challenge can be decided under existing precedent, that precedent is not reconsidered.
